appraisal_events.evidence: The salon that an hour ago breathed "un goût vrai pour l'art et même une sorte de noblesse morale" now shows him "ses ridicules, sa sottise, son ignominie"; "Quelle gaîté fétide !", "les plaisanteries d'une Verdurin", "Idiote, menteuse ! et ça croit aimer l'Art !", "maquerelle, entremetteuse !" over the seat she will make for Forcheville beside Odette.
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann pours contempt on Mme Verdurin and her clan, but the passage explicitly dates the reversal to the moment another man gained free access to Odette there, so the narration reports the verdict without crediting it.

appraisal_events.evidence: He speaks aloud "sur le même ton un peu factice" he used to praise the little nucleus; he draws himself up — "J'habite à trop de milliers de mètres d'altitude…" — and invokes his mission to raise Odette, "comme si cette mission… datait de plus longtemps que de quelques minutes, et comme s'il ne se l'était pas donnée seulement depuis qu'il pensait que ces sarcasmes l'avaient peut-être lui-même pour objet".
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator dismantles Swann's moral posture in the same breath in which he strikes it, exposing the loftiness, the disgust, and the rescue mission as improvised jealousy of a few minutes' standing.

appraisal_events.evidence: He pictures her overdressed for a day in the country, "car elle est si vulgaire et surtout, la pauvre petite, elle est tellement bête !!!", and asks how a creature made in God's image can find matter for laughter in such jokes.
appraisal_events.explanation: The same jealous swing turns on Odette herself, and the woman he means to raise into a purer atmosphere is called vulgar and stupid; the narrative frame that discredits his indignation covers this judgment too.

status_effects.explanation: He walks home alone rehearsing an evening at which Odette will be free with another man and at which he may himself become the joke she laughs at — all the leverage in the relation has passed away from him.
The clan reconstitutes at Chatou without him, with Forcheville installed in the place beside Odette that the hostess used to make for him; he is now outside a circle he was inside.
The narrator shows his elevated disgust to be a factitious pose invented minutes earlier, so the tirade lowers the speaker rather than its objects.
She is called an idiot, a liar, a procuress and a fraud about art; the abuse marks her locally even though the passage discredits the man delivering it.
She is judged vulgar and stupid by the man who loves her, in the same interior monologue that claims to want to raise her.

ambiguities: Every appraisal here is Swann's imagining of an evening that has not happened, and the narrator dates his revulsion to the minutes since he suspected the clan's sarcasm was aimed at him — so the diminishments of Mme Verdurin and Odette are recorded as locally staged, not as narration-backed verdicts.
